content_voiceover: This table gives the actual prevalence data behind the classic TTP pentad, and these numbers are worth memorizing because boards love asking which feature is most common versus least common. Neurologic symptoms are very common overall, headache and confusion occur in about sixty percent of patients, and if you break neurologic findings down, mild deficits like headache or confusion occur in about twenty five percent while severe findings, coma, focal deficits, or seizures, occur in fully fifty percent, so when neurologic involvement happens in TTP it tends to be severe. Renal involvement is the opposite pattern, mild proteinuria or renal insufficiency is common at forty percent, but severe acute renal failure is uncommon, only about five percent, which is a key differentiator from HUS where renal failure dominates. Digestive symptoms, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, occur in about half of patients and can mimic other diagnoses early on. Bleeding symptoms like purpura or menorrhagia are seen in only twenty percent, since TTP is primarily a thrombotic, not a hemorrhagic, disorder despite the low platelet count. And the hematologic numbers are dramatic, platelet counts under twenty times ten to the ninth per liter in ninety five percent of patients, and hemoglobin under eight in eighty percent, reflecting severe consumptive thrombocytopenia and hemolysis.
keypoints: Headache/confusion ~60%; severe neuro findings (coma, seizures, focal deficits) ~50%
Severe renal failure only ~5% in TTP, unlike HUS
Bleeding symptoms only ~20% -- TTP is thrombotic, not hemorrhagic
keypoint_voiceover: Lock in these TTP prevalence numbers for boards, headache or confusion in sixty percent, with severe neurologic findings like coma or seizures in fully half of patients. Renal failure is usually mild, severe renal failure occurs in only about five percent, which helps distinguish TTP from HUS. Platelets drop below twenty in ninety five percent of patients and hemoglobin falls below eight in eighty percent, while overt bleeding is uncommon at only twenty percent.
